sections.h: Jacob's tithe and the second tithe (Jubilees 32)
sections.b: Jubilees tells how Jacob paid the tenth he vowed at Bethel (Genesis 28:22): a tenth of people, animals, gold and clothing, with his tenth son, Levi, given to God as priest (Jubilees 32:2–9). The angel then gives the law of a "tithe again," the second tithe of grain, wine and oil, eaten before the Lord each year at the chosen place and burned if kept past the next harvest (Jubilees 32:10–14), and assigns the tithe of herds and flocks to the priests (Jubilees 32:15; compare Leviticus 27:32). Like Tobit 1:7, Jubilees reads the law of Moses as asking for more than one tithe, and says these laws were written on the heavenly tablets before Sinai.
sections.refs: Genesis 28:22; Deuteronomy 14:22–26; Leviticus 27:30–32; Numbers 18:21–26; Tobit 1:7; Jubilees 32:2–15

uncommon: Jubilees counts a person among Jacob's tenths: Levi, the tenth son counted upward from the unborn Benjamin (Jubilees 32:3).

sections.b: In Jubilees the priesthood begins before Sinai. Levi dreams that he is made "a priest of God Most High," Melchizedek's title (Genesis 14:18), and Jacob dresses him in priestly clothes and "filled his hands," the ordination phrase of Exodus 28:41 (Jubilees 32:1–3). Levi offers the sacrifices of the Feast of Booths at Bethel and receives the unclean animals and the tithe of herds (Jubilees 32:8–15). The Testament of Levi 8–9 tells the same dream. Hebrews 7:9–10 reads the same chapters of Genesis the other way: Levi, still in Abraham's body, paid tithes to Melchizedek. Israel too is called "a kingdom of priests" (Jubilees 33:20; Exodus 19:6).
sections.refs: Genesis 14:18–20; Exodus 28:41; Exodus 19:6; Hebrews 7:9–10; Jubilees 32:1–15; Jubilees 33:20

sections.b: Jubilees keeps Jacob's altar and feast at Bethel, and Levi's ordination there, but forbids a lasting sanctuary. When Jacob plans to wall in the place and make it holy forever, an angel with seven tablets tells him, "this is not the place" (Jubilees 32:16–22). The book thus reconciles Genesis 28:22, "will become a house of God," with Deuteronomy's one place God chooses (Deuteronomy 12:5), and leaves no patriarchal warrant for the later shrine at Bethel (1 Kings 12:29).

Jacob keeps the seven days of Booths at Bethel, from the fifteenth of the seventh month, and then one more day, which he names "Addition" (Jubilees 32:4–7, 27–29). It is the closing assembly of Leviticus 23:36 and Numbers 29:35. Charles thought the Ge'ez name came from a miscopied Greek word, and that the Latin "a keeping back" is nearer the original: Jacob was "kept back" a day at Bethel. The offerings are counted in sevens, unlike the pattern of Numbers 29.

Jubilees dates Benjamin's birth to the eleventh of the eighth month and has Rachel name him "Son of My Pain," the meaning of Genesis' Ben-oni (Jubilees 32:33; Genesis 35:18). She is buried "in the land of Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem," with Jacob's standing stone over her grave (Jubilees 32:34). Bilhah, her slave woman, is later buried across from Rachel's tomb (Jubilees 34:16).
sections.refs: Genesis 35:16–20; Genesis 48:7; Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18; Jubilees 32:33–34; Jubilees 34:16

sections.b: Jubilees says the laws were written on the heavenly tablets from the beginning, and the patriarchs kept many of them. But when it tells of Reuben and Bilhah it must explain why Reuben was not put to death as Leviticus 20:11 requires. Its answer: "until then the ordinance, the judgment and the law had not been revealed in full for everyone" (Jubilees 33:16). Now, in Moses' days, the law is complete and eternal, and "Let no one say" that Reuben's case is a precedent (Jubilees 33:15). Charles compared Romans 4:15 and Romans 5:13, though Paul draws the opposite lesson.
sections.refs: Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 20:11; Romans 4:15; Romans 5:13–14; Galatians 3:19; Jubilees 33:10–20

common: Jubilees teaches that the patriarchs knew and kept laws later given to Moses.
uncommon: Jubilees itself admits that some laws, with their penalties, were not revealed until Moses (Jubilees 33:16).

sections.b: After Reuben's sin with Bilhah, Jubilees says, "There is no greater sin than the sexual sin they commit on the earth," because Israel is "a holy nation ... a kingdom of priests" (Jubilees 33:20). The book ranks sexual impurity, with marriage to the nations (Jubilees 30), as the chief threat to Israel's holiness. Paul sets sexual sin apart too (1 Corinthians 6:18) but does not rank it above every other sin.

sections.h: The Day of Atonement and Joseph's brothers (Jubilees 34)
sections.b: Leviticus 16 gives no event behind the fast of the tenth day of the seventh month. Jubilees gives one: on that day Jacob's sons sent him Joseph's robe dipped in a goat's blood, and he wept. "That is why" Israel afflicts itself and makes atonement with a young goat on that day, once a year, "for they had grieved their father's tender love for his son Joseph" (Jubilees 34:12–19). Charles noted that rabbinic tradition knows nothing of this origin. The Mishnah teaches that the Day atones for sins against another only once that person is appeased (Mishnah Yoma 8:9), and Hebrews reads the yearly repetition as a reminder of sins (Hebrews 10:3).

uncommon: Jubilees ties the Day of Atonement to the sale of Joseph: the brothers' goat of deceit and Israel's goat of atonement fall on the same date (Jubilees 34:12, 18).

sections.b: Jubilees tells the sale of Joseph briefly: Jacob sends him from home to Shechem, he finds his brothers at Dothan, they plot to kill him, then sell him to Ishmaelite traders, who sell him to Potiphar, "Pharaoh's eunuch, the chief of the cooks, priest of the city of Elew" (Jubilees 34:10–11). Potiphar here is merged with Potiphera, priest of On (Genesis 41:45). The robe reaches Jacob on the tenth of the seventh month, the date that becomes the Day of Atonement (Jubilees 34:12, 18).

sections.h: Jacob kills Esau: the war of Jubilees 37–38
sections.b: Genesis ends the twins' story in peace (Genesis 33:4; 35:29). Jubilees adds a war. After Isaac's death Esau's sons, angry that Jacob has the birthright, force Esau to lead an army of four thousand from Aram, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, the Horites and the Kittim against Jacob's tower near Hebron (Jubilees 37). Esau breaks the oath he swore to his parents; Jacob shoots him with an arrow, his sons rout the army, and Edom is put under tribute "to this day" (Jubilees 38:1–14). Charles found the legend also in the Testament of Judah 9 and in medieval Hebrew collections, and linked its final form to John Hyrcanus' conquest of Idumea.
sections.refs: Genesis 27:40; Genesis 33:4; Genesis 36:6–8; Deuteronomy 23:7; 2 Samuel 8:14; Jubilees 37:1–38:14

uncommon: In Jubilees Esau is killed by Jacob's arrow (Jubilees 38:2); later Jewish tradition gave the deed to Hushim son of Dan.

sections.b: Genesis remembers Leah as "the unloved one" (Genesis 29:31). Jubilees ends her life differently: after Rachel's death Jacob "loved her very much," because she was "blameless and upright in all her ways," never spoke a harsh word, and honored him (Jubilees 36:21–24). She is buried in the double cave beside Rebekah, as Genesis 49:31 says, and Esau's attack comes while Jacob mourns her (Jubilees 37:14).

Jubilees gives Isaac a farewell speech: do what is right, love your brothers as your own souls, reject idols, remember the God of Abraham. He makes his sons swear by God's great name never to plan evil against each other, and warns that the one who does will fall into his brother's hand (Jubilees 36:1–11). He dies glad, aged 180, as in Genesis 35:28–29, after Joseph's sale, which agrees with Genesis' own numbers.

Isaac tells Rebekah, "Jacob's guardian is great, mighty and honored, and praised above Esau's guardian" (Jubilees 35:17). Charles called this the earliest distinct reference to a person's guardian angel, the belief behind Matthew 18:10 and Acts 12:15. The words could also mean God himself, who promised to guard Jacob (Genesis 28:15), set against a lesser power over Esau, like the princes of the nations in Daniel 10.
sections.refs: Genesis 28:15; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20–21; Matthew 18:10; Acts 12:15; Hebrews 1:14; Jubilees 35:17

sections.h: The book of life and the book of destruction (Jubilees 36)
sections.b: Isaac warns that whoever plans evil against his brother "will be blotted out of the book of the instruction of humankind. He will not be entered in the book of life, but in the book of those who perish" (Jubilees 36:10). Jubilees thus has two heavenly books, one of life and one of destruction, like the books opened in Revelation 20:12.

sections.h: Jacob's vow paid, Esau's oath broken
sections.b: Jubilees tells how Jacob paid his Bethel vow with a tenth of everything and seven days of offerings (Jubilees 32:2–9; Genesis 28:20–22). Later Esau swears to his mother and to Isaac by God's great name to love his brother (Jubilees 35:24; 36:7–8), and breaks the oath when his sons force him to war (Jubilees 37:13, 17). The story shows a vow kept and an oath broken, and their outcomes.
sections.refs: Genesis 28:20–22; Numbers 30:2; Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12; Jubilees 32:2–9; Jubilees 35:24; Jubilees 37:13

sections.h: Hasmonean wars in the stories of Jacob? (Jubilees 34; 37–38)
sections.b: Charles read Jacob's wars as old legends retold with the geography of the writer's age. The Amorite kings' towns include Tappuah (Tephon), Hazor, Beth-horon and Timnath, places of the Maccabean campaigns (Jubilees 34:4–8; 1 Maccabees 9:50). Esau dies at Aduram, which Charles identified with Adora, one of the Idumean towns John Hyrcanus took when he subdued the Idumeans (Jubilees 38:8; Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1). Edom serves Jacob's sons "to this day" (Jubilees 38:14). Scholars who date the book before Hyrcanus read these as older traditions.

Isaac gives the firstborn's larger share, with Abraham's tower and his goods at Beersheba; Esau declares that he sold his birthright to Jacob and gives up all claim (Jubilees 36:12–15). After Isaac's death Esau tells his angry sons the story of Genesis 25 and 27 fairly: he sold the birthright "for a little lentil stew," and Jacob came "with cunning" for the blessing (Jubilees 37:3). His sons will not accept it, and the war follows.

Jubilees calls Dinah "Jacob's only daughter" (Jubilees 33:22) and says she died in the month Joseph was lost, and was buried near Rachel's tomb with Bilhah (Jubilees 34:15–16). Genesis does not tell her death. Later rabbinic tradition married her to Simeon (Genesis Rabbah 80; Charles notes it).

Rebekah tells Jacob, "I have seen the day of my death in a dream," and that she will not live beyond 155 years; Jacob laughs, for she is still strong, but she dies that year (Jubilees 35:6–8, 27). Earlier in the same part Levi dreams that he is made a priest at Bethel (Jubilees 32:1), and Jacob sees the seven tablets "in a vision of the night" (Jubilees 32:21).

sections.h: Tithes, a feast day and a marriage law on the tablets (Jubilees 32-33)
sections.b: In this part the heavenly tablets hold the law of the second tithe and the herd tithe (Jubilees 32:10, 15), the eighth day of Booths (Jubilees 32:28), and the death penalty for lying with a father's wife (Jubilees 33:10). Jacob is also shown seven tablets by an angel, on which he reads the future of his family, and he writes what he read (Jubilees 32:21-26). Origen quotes a lost Prayer of Joseph in which Jacob says he "read in the tablets of heaven" what would happen to his sons (as Charles prints it).
